The position is mate in 2 for White. The only checking move that forces mate against every legal reply is 1.Qd6-d8+. This places the queen on the eighth rank with a clear path (e8 and f8 empty), checking the king along the rank.

Black has no interpositions (no piece can reach e8 or f8 in one move) and no king escapes (both f8 and h8 remain attacked by the queen on d8). The sole legal reply is therefore 1...Rc8xd8.

White then plays 2.Rb8xd8#. The rook on d8 checks along the eighth rank (e8 and f8 empty). Black has:
- no captures on d8 (queen on a6 does not attack d8; knight on b6 does not attack d8; king does not attack d8; no pawns attack d8);
- no king escapes (f8 and h8 are attacked by the rook on d8; f7, g7 and h7 are occupied by Black's own pawns);
- no interpositions (queen cannot reach e8 or f8; knight cannot reach e8 or f8; no pawns can reach the eighth rank).

All other first-move checks (Qd6-f8+ or Rb8-c8+) allow Black at least one reply that prevents immediate mate on the second move, so they do not solve the puzzle.

- The king cannot capture because d6 is protected by the e5-pawn (and moving the king there would be illegal).

- The rook on b3 does not attack d6 (not aligned on rank or file).

Black therefore has only four legal king moves that escape the check: c7, c8, e7, or e8. In every case the bishop on d5 remains hanging and unprotected.

White's second move is therefore d6d5, capturing the bishop. None of Black's possible king destinations attack d5, and no other black unit protects d5, so the capture is safe and wins a full piece. This is the principal variation that realizes the fork.

The position features a classic knight fork on g5. White's knight on f3 moves to g5, delivering check to the king on h7 while simultaneously attacking the rook on f7. Black's only way to resolve the check is to capture the knight with the queen (f4g5), as no other black piece attacks g5 and knight checks cannot be blocked. This capture is forced because alternatives (such as moving the king) allow White to capture the now-undefended queen on f4 with the rook on f1, leading to even greater material loss for Black. White then recaptures the queen with Qg3xg5. The net result is that White wins the queen for the knight (a decisive material gain). Other first-move candidates, such as Qg3xf4, lead only to an even queen trade after Rf7xf4 and do not exploit the fork or the discovered attack along the f-file. The three-ply line therefore represents the main variation that realizes the fork tactic.

e4g5 f4g5 e7e3
The best continuation begins with the knight check e4g5. This move checks the white king on f3 while simultaneously clearing the e4 square, uncovering an attack by the rook on e7 against the white rook on e3.

White's most resilient reply is to capture the checking knight with f4g5. Black then captures the hanging rook with e7e3. This is check (the rook on e3 attacks horizontally along the third rank to the king on f3), forcing White to resolve the check.

The resulting position allows Black to maintain material parity after the forced sequence of rook trades (e2e3 e8e3 f3xe3) while retaining the possibility of further gains (e.g., via Qc4xd3 followed by recapturing with the rook on e3). Alternative White replies (king moves to f2 or g2) allow Black to emerge a full knight ahead after the same rook trades. Thus e4g5 f4g5 e7e3 is the main line that secures Black's advantage.

e4g3 f1f3 g3f5
The position features a powerful knight fork available to Black. The knight on e4 can move to g3, which attacks both the white queen on f1 and the white rook on f5. The g3 square is completely safe: it is not attacked by any white piece (the g2-pawn blocks the queen's line, and no other unit controls g3).

White's only reasonable reply is to move the queen to a square that both escapes the fork and continues to protect the rook on f5. The unique square satisfying these conditions is f3:
- The path f1-f2-f3 is clear.
- From f3 the queen still sees f5 along the open f-file.
- f3 itself is not attacked by any black unit.

After Qf3 Black simply captures the undefended rook with Ng3xf5. White will recapture on the next move, but the net result is that Black has won the exchange (rook for knight). All other white replies to the fork lose even more material, confirming that e4g3 f1f3 g3f5 is the main line.

The move Qf5-f8 is check (queen on the 8th rank with clear path to the king) and simultaneously attacks the rook on g7 along the diagonal (creating a relative pin to the h6-pawn). Black has only two legal replies to the check:

- Moving the king to b7 allows Qf8xg7, winning the rook (which has no defenders).
- Blocking with the knight (c7-e8) is the lesser evil. The knight on e8 is undefended, so the follow-up Qf8xe8 wins the knight.

Black therefore chooses the knight block to lose only a minor piece rather than a rook. The three-ply line forces the win of a knight.

d4f6 h4h5 h8h7
The position has Black in check from the bishop on f6. The only way to resolve the check while creating a decisive threat is 1...d4f6, which captures the checking piece and simultaneously places the bishop on a diagonal that checks the white king on h4 (path f6-g5-h4 is clear).

White's only legal replies are king moves that escape the check: 2.Kh4h3 or 2.Kh4h5. Both squares remain on the h-file, so the absolute pin of the white queen on h7 to the king (by the rook on h8) is preserved. No interposition is possible on g5, and the queen cannot capture on f6 or leave the h-file without exposing the king.

After either king move, 3...h8h7 captures the pinned queen. The queen is undefended on h7 (neither king destination attacks h7, and no other white unit does), so Black wins the queen for a bishop. Other ways of resolving the initial check (e.g., 1...Ke7f6) allow White to capture the rook safely and are therefore inferior.

This simultaneously attacks the queen on f7 and pins it to the black king on g8, as any departure of the queen from the diagonal would allow the bishop to deliver check along the now-unobstructed path. This pins the rook because any move by the rook would expose the king to check from the bishop. White's king must move to break the pin and retain protection of the rook (only e3 and f2 achieve this). After e2e3, Black captures the pinned rook with g4f3. The bishop on f3 is protected by nothing and is recaptured by the king, but Black has won a rook for a bishop (net material gain). This is the principal line under best play, as alternative White responses (such as d4d5) allow Black to reposition the rook first and still force the same material gain on the next move.

The key move is the check 1. Re5, forcing Black's bishop to capture and removing it from g7. This activates the pin on the f7-pawn (now attacked by the queen on h7 with the king behind on the 7th rank). White then captures the pinning rook on g6 with 2. Qxg6. Black is forced to recapture with the f7-pawn (the only legal capturer), as ignoring it allows White to capture the hanging queen on h3 with the g2-pawn (the pin on g2 having been broken by the loss of the g6-rook). The net result is a pawn up with a dominant position. Other Black defenses to the initial check (interpositions on e6) allow White to win the queen for a rook or more.

The black bishop on d5 is pinned to the queen on f7 by the white bishop on c4. White captures the pinned bishop with the rook (d6d5). Black's queen must recapture (f7d5) or lose the bishop for nothing. White then captures the queen with the pinning bishop (c4d5). This is check, and the d5-bishop is protected by the queen on d4. Black can capture it with the c6-pawn, but White recaptures with the queen on the next move, remaining up a queen and pawn for a rook after the full sequence (with further gains possible against the a8-rook). Capturing the bishop first with the queen or bishop leads to inferior or equivalent results under best defense; starting with the rook directly exploits the pin with the existing attacker.

The only checking move is the knight capture on the hanging bishop. After f7h6 the black king has two legal squares. Kg7 allows a follow-up that wins a rook plus a pawn for a knight (net +6), so the superior defense is Kh8.  

The reply h6f7 is then the strongest continuation: it clears the h-file, creating a double check (knight + rook). Black cannot capture on f7 with the f8-rook because that would leave the king in check from the rook on h1; the king must therefore move. White has already secured the bishop and keeps both knights, with further pressure on the f8-rook available on the next move.  

All other second-move tries either allow Black to trade the rook for a knight or permit Black a tempo to save the rook or give check with the b5-bishop. The three-ply line therefore represents best play for both sides.

The position has White's bishop on f7 delivering check to Black's king on g8. This bishop is unprotected, making it a hanging piece that Black can safely capture with the king.

After 1...g8f7, White's most effective response is 2.h4f6+, placing the queen on f6 with check (vertical alignment to the king on f7, path clear). This check cannot be captured (f6 is protected by the e5-pawn) and cannot be blocked (adjacent squares).

Black's only legal replies are king moves to safe squares not attacked by the queen on f6: e8 or g8. Moving to e8 allows White to follow up with Qxg6+ and later Qxf5, regaining two pawns while the king is driven to d8. Moving to g8 allows the same pawn captures but keeps the f8-bishop on the board longer, limiting White's additional gains. Thus 3...f7g8 is the most resilient choice, leaving Black up a bishop for two pawns after the main continuation 4.Qf6xg6+ f8g7 5.Qg6xf5.

This line captures the hanging piece on the first ply and forces White's best counter-check while preserving Black's material edge. All other king escapes or non-capturing first moves lose more material.

The white rook on d2 is hanging and unprotected. Black's best move is Qg5xd2, which captures the rook and delivers check along the second rank (path e2-f2 clear). White has no way to capture the checking queen. The only legal responses are king moves or interposition. Interposing with the queen on e2 allows Black to capture it safely (e2 unprotected), but interposing on f2 (f3f2) blocks the check and protects the square with the king. Black must then capture the queen (d2f2) rather than divert to other targets, as failing to do so allows White's queen to capture on d2 next. This sequence wins a rook outright; the second hanging rook on c4 can be collected on the subsequent move after White recaptures on f2. Alternative first moves (e.g., d5c4) allow White to force a queen trade and only equalize material.

The black queen on h3 is hanging to the g2-pawn but the pawn is pinned to the white king by the rook on g8. Moving the king to h1 breaks the pin without entering check (h1 is not attacked by any black unit). This creates an immediate threat of g2xh3, winning the queen.

Black's only way to avoid losing the queen is to move it to a safe square. All safe squares (h4, f5, e6, d7, c8) leave the knight on e3 undefended. The knight was protected solely by the queen; once the queen leaves h3 the knight becomes hanging.

White therefore captures the undefended knight with the rook. The resulting rook on e3 cannot be recaptured because none of the safe queen squares attack e3, and no other black unit protects e3. White therefore nets a full knight for no compensation. 

Alternative king moves (e.g. Kf2) allow Black defensive resources that reduce White's net gain; Kh1 is the only move that forces the full win of the knight against best defense.
